extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity officers, and policymakers interested in retractions and publication ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive, bibliometric, and temporal analysis of retracted medical publications (1975–2024) using the Retraction Watch Database, with categorization of retraction reasons, geographic and journal-level breakdowns, and recommendations for improving research integrity and editorial processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data inclusion and exclusion criteria for retraction dataset
rubrics_metrics.description: Medicine and medicine-related publications were extracted from the Retraction Watch Database; records labelled as 'correction', 'expression of concern', and 'reinstatement' were excluded; duplicate publications were removed based on title; publications with zero days between publication and retraction were excluded; retractions from 2025 were removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact filtering steps: 1) initial medicine-only filtering via Python script, 2) remove non-retraction types (corrections, expressions of concern, reinstatements), 3) deduplicate by title, 4) exclude records with zero days between publication and retraction (data-integrity concern), 5) exclude future-year retractions. These steps improve reproducibility and dataset validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and categorization of retraction reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction reasons were extracted and organized into unique categories: 106 unique categories initially identified then reduced (excluding metadata-like reason categories) to 68 categories; related subcategories were presented together (not merged) and counts summed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use automated scripts to extract unique reason strings, exclude administrative/meta categories (investigating party, notice quality), present subgrouping transparently without unjustified merging, and document mapping decisions (the authors provide Supplementary Data 2: Python script for categorization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Top retraction reason — Data concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues with data integrity or unreliable results (recorded as the leading reason; examples/subcategories include: unreliable results, concerns/issues about data, concerns/issues about results, concerns about images, unreliable data, results not reproducible, unreliable image, contamination of cell lines/tissues/materials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report counts and percentages; visualize temporal trends; consider that data concerns may reflect detection improvements as well as real changes in data integrity. In analyses, treat multiple reason-tags per article appropriately (multiple-count recording).

rubrics_metrics.name: Top retraction reason — Fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate deception in research conduct (examples/subcategories: paper mills, falsification/fabrication of data, false/forged authorship, manipulation of images, rogue editor, falsification/fabrication of image/results, false affiliation, hoax paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disaggregate subtypes when possible (e.g., paper mills vs falsified data); quantify growth rates (authors estimated doubling every ~5.2 years for fraud); interpret in context of detection tools and editorial oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top retraction reason — Peer review issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Compromised peer review processes, including fake reviews and reviewer manipulation (listed as a major retraction reason).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track specific subcategories (fake peer review vs general concerns); temporal trends may be steep but require statistical testing (the authors reported a high annual rate but no statistical significance for peer-review issues in one model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Top retraction reason — Referencing issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Improper citation practices or reference manipulation to increase impact; includes citing retracted work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count both broad referencing concerns and specific acts (e.g., citing retracted work) and report as percent of reasons; consider interaction with misconduct and fraud categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top retraction reason — Ethical issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of research ethics including lack of IRB/IACUC approval, absence/withdrawal of informed/patient consent, concerns about human subject welfare, ethical violations by author/third party, lack of institutional/company approval, animal welfare concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report subcategory breakdowns (e.g., % lacking IRB approvals). In medicine, ethical issues have direct implications for patient safety; treat these reasons as distinct from methodological errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top retraction reason — Duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication of substantially overlapping content across journals or within the same journal; includes duplication of article, image, data, and text, as well as duplicate publications via publisher error and euphemisms for duplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate intentional duplicate publication from publisher/journal errors; report counts for images vs text vs data duplication; consider co-occurrence with plagiarism or paper mills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top retraction reason — Error
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine mistakes requiring retraction: errors in data, analyses, methods, results/conclusions, images, text, materials, cell lines/tissues; also errors by journal/publisher or third-party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate honest errors from misconduct; include publisher-caused errors separately; report median time-to-retraction for errors vs misconduct categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top retraction reason — Plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Unattributed use of others’ work, ideas, or language (subcategories: plagiarism of article/text/image/data, euphemisms for plagiarism, taken from dissertation/thesis, taken via peer review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify explicit plagiarism vs euphemistic labels; quantify and report subtypes; use similarity-detection tools in editorial screening to reduce incidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top retraction reason — Randomly generated content (AI-generated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles created using artificial intelligence tools without proper review or verification (classified separately among top reasons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag and quantify AI-generated content as a distinct reason; recommend verification and manual checks to detect nonsensical or machine-generated submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top retraction reason — Misconduct (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: General research misconduct not specified in other categories, including misconduct by author, misconduct found via official investigation, misconduct by third party or company, and euphemisms for misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report as a catch-all but disaggregate when official investigation findings are available; consider overlap with fraud and data concerns in correlation analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive and inferential statistical analysis standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Use descriptive statistics (numbers, percentages, means, standard deviations, medians, minimums, maximums). For temporal trend analysis, if linear model fit is poor use semi-logarithmic linear regression (log-transform counts) and report growth rates, confidence intervals, B coefficients, R^2, and p-values. Use Spearman's rank correlation to assess monotonic relationships between retraction reasons and year. Use χ2 analysis for categorical distribution comparisons (e.g., WoS-indexed vs non-indexed) and report odds ratios where appropriate. Set statistical significance at P < 0.05 and indicate multiple significance levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document modeling choices (why log-transform was used), report effect sizes and uncertainty, and choose nonparametric correlation when variables are not normally distributed. Present visualization (line graphs, correlation matrices) alongside statistical tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data quality and time-to-retraction metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute and report time between publication and retraction (median, range). Exclude suspicious entries such as zero-day intervals as potential data-integrity issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report distribution of time-to-retraction and consider stratifying by reason (e.g., fraud vs error) and by journal type (WoS vs non-WoS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing checks and journal-level analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine PubMed indexing rates by checking for retraction notice or PMID; assess Web of Science indexing by converting DOIs into batch queries; compare distributions of retracted articles across indexed vs non-indexed sources with χ2 tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report percent indexed, counts per source, and test for differences; provide per-journal retraction counts and identify concentration in a small number of sources (e.g., top 10 sources contributing ~30% of retractions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical distribution and visualization standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Create choropleth maps to visualize global distribution of retracted publications (authors used Natural Earth dataset, geopandas, and matplotlib).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reliable base maps (Natural Earth), document country-counting rules (multi-country authored papers counted in each applicable country), and present heatmaps alongside tabulated country counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling multiple reason-tags per article
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles may have multiple retraction reasons; counts and percentages reflect multiple reason-tags per article (48,649 reason counts for 16,041 publications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting proportions, clarify whether denominators are reasons-counts or publication-counts and ensure transparent reporting of multi-reason attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and use of public data
rubrics_metrics.description: When using publicly available databases (Retraction Watch Database), formal ethical approval may not be required as no human subjects or patient-level data are involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State ethical considerations explicitly in methods and include data-sharing statements; if any non-public or sensitive data are used, seek appropriate approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial screening processes to reduce misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should adopt more stringent editorial practices by integrating comprehensive screening procedures to detect plagiarism, image manipulation, and fabricated data and utilizing advanced software tools before the peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement automated screening (similarity checking, image forensics, statistical anomaly detection) pre-peer-review; document screening thresholds and escalation procedures for suspected issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor training and standardized checklists
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may benefit from receiving formal training to recognize indicators of scientific misconduct and employing standardized checklists throughout the article evaluation process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide case-based training, protocols for responding to suspected misconduct, and standardized evaluation checklists to reduce editorial oversight variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review process safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Enhance peer-review by using verified reviewers’ databases, implementing double-blind or open peer-review procedures, and avoiding reliance on reviewers suggested by authors to reduce manipulation and fake reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt reviewer identity verification, maintain curated reviewer pools, and consider blinded review formats or transparent open-review models; establish policies limiting or vetting author-suggested reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional research-ethics education and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic institutions and universities should provide comprehensive training in research ethics to all graduate and postgraduate students, emphasizing case-based learning, transparency, data management, and publishing ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop mandatory curricula for ethics, data stewardship, and reproducibility; use real-case analyses and assess competency; document training uptake and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic incentive and cultural change
rubrics_metrics.description: Foster a shift in academic culture from metrics focusing on output (quantity) to assessments prioritizing quality and integrity to reduce pressures that contribute to unethical behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform hiring/promotion/funding criteria to reward reproducibility, data sharing, and research integrity; monitor effects of incentive changes on publication behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-layered strategy for sustaining research reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ multi-layered strategies combining editorial screening, peer-review reform, institutional training, and cultural incentives to maintain the long-term reliability of medical research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate efforts across stakeholders (journals, institutions, funders) and evaluate interventions longitudinally using metrics such as retraction rates by reason, time-to-retraction, and detection-to-retraction intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent reporting and reproducible methods (scripts and supplementary materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide processing scripts and methods (authors supplied Python scripts for filtering, categorizing reasons, and geographical analysis as supplementary materials) to ensure reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share code and exact mapping rules (e.g., Supplementary Data 1–3) so other researchers can reproduce filtering, categorization, and visualizations; document software versions and parameters.
